claims.text: Applying an atmospheric-plasma-sprayed AlCoCrFeNi HEA coating followed by annealing at 550 °C for 2 h will suppress corrosion-related degradation of Q235 steel.
Annealing the coating at 550 °C for 2 h generates a dense, refined microstructure.
The annealed coating rapidly forms stable Al- and Cr-rich passive oxide or hydroxide layers.
The dense, refined coating and its passive layers reduce pit initiation and corrosive-ion ingress under room-temperature acidic and high-temperature salt exposure.
Annealing at 550 °C produces an average coating grain size near 15 µm.
The coating annealed at 550 °C has predominantly low-angle grain boundaries.
The coating retains a major BCC phase after annealing at 550 °C.
The annealed microstructure promotes formation of Cr2O3, Fe(OH)3, Cr(OH)3, and Co(OH)2 during corrosive exposure.
Microstructural refinement increases coating hardness and limits dislocation motion.
Stable Al- and Cr-rich passive oxides impede pitting and crack propagation by blocking penetration of corrosive species.
Annealing above 550 °C may cause grain growth and unfavorable phase transitions that reduce the coating's protective effects.
The coating annealed at 550 °C will have higher microhardness than untreated Q235 steel and the as-sprayed coated reference.
The coating annealed at 550 °C will exhibit a less negative corrosion potential, lower corrosion current, and higher polarization resistance than both reference groups.
The coating annealed at 550 °C will exhibit lower cyclic weight gain during 900 °C hot-corrosion testing than both reference groups.
The predicted corrosion suppression applies to an approximately 150 µm coating tested in 3.5 wt% H2SO4 at room temperature and defined Na2SO4/NaCl/V2O5 mixtures at 900 °C.
Evidence from analogous SS316L systems supports the effectiveness of the proposed coating and annealing strategy.
Differences between SS316L and Q235 substrates may alter interfacial behavior and the degree of corrosion suppression.
